docs.title: Experiments at the Institute of Control Systems
docs.text:
This page lists the experimental setups running in our lab: what each one is, what state it is in, and who looks after it. Each entry links to a page with a fuller description, photographs, and what is currently open on it.

If you are a student looking for a thesis or project topic, start at For students.

docs.text:

About the source links

Repository links point to our internal GitLab. If you are not a member of the institute the link will show a "not found" page — that is expected, not a broken link.

docs.title: Status meanings
docs.text:
• Running — the setup works and can be used today.
  • In progress — being built or substantially reworked; parts may not work.
  • In preparation — planned, hardware may not exist yet.
  • Dormant — the hardware exists but nobody is currently working on it. Often a good place to start.

docs.title: For students
docs.text: We supervise Bachelor's and Master's theses, project work, and research internships on the setups listed on the overview page.

docs.title: How to choose something
docs.text:
Each experiment page has a section called What is open. Those are real, currently unclaimed pieces of work, not a wish list. Read two or three pages, pick the one where that section makes you want to try something, and contact the owner named at the top of the page.

You do not need to already know how to do the thing. You do need to be able to say why it interests you.

docs.title: What to expect
docs.text: Work on these setups is part theory and part hardware. Something will not work the first time — that is the normal state of an experiment, not a sign that anything has gone wrong.

docs.title: Contact
docs.text: Write to the owner listed on the experiment page. If you are not sure which setup fits, write to the institute and say roughly what you find interesting.

docs.title: Raspbot V2 mecanum platform
docs.text: Status Running Owner TBD Last reviewed 2026-09 Source Repository (institute members only)

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
A small four-wheeled robot with mecanum wheels, driven by a Raspberry Pi. It serves as a scaled-down stand-in for a heavy-load transport trolley: the kinematics are the same, the mass and the consequences of a mistake are not. Because the wheels are omnidirectional, the platform can translate sideways and rotate independently, which makes it a convenient testbed for setpoint tracking and formation control ideas before they touch anything large.

Photograph of the platform goes here.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text:
• Yahboom Raspbot V2 chassis, four mecanum wheels
  • Raspberry Pi 4B as the on-board computer
  • Motor driver co-processor addressed over I²C
  • No wheel encoders and no IMU in the stock configuration

docs.title: Software
docs.text:
• Ubuntu Server with ROS 2 on the Pi
  • MATLAB with the ROS Toolbox on the operator machine
  • Camera-based pose estimation using fiducial markers

docs.title: What has been done
docs.text:
• Motor control over I²C is working; all four wheels can be driven independently.
  • The mapping from commanded wheel speeds to physical motion has been characterised empirically, since the platform has no encoders to measure it.
  • A localisation approach based on fiducial markers has been selected and the camera calibration prepared.

docs.title: What is open
docs.text:
Concrete things a student could pick up:

  • Closed-loop velocity control. The platform is open-loop today. Adding encoders means selecting an encoder-capable driver board and rebuilding the low-level control accordingly.
  • Pose estimation. Fusing marker-based absolute measurements with dead reckoning, and quantifying how well it actually holds up during motion.
  • Formation control. Once two platforms track setpoints reliably, running a distributed controller across both.
